Root cause: applicationWillTerminate called CefShutdown() directly while CefBrowser instances were still alive (CEF requires CloseBrowser + OnBeforeClose for every browser first). Fixed by overriding -[NSApplication terminate:] in Sources/Bridge/BRWApplication.mm (matching CEF's own cefclient/cefsimple reference pattern) to force-close all browsers via a new BRWClientHandler registry (CloseAll/LiveCount), poll to completion on the existing +[BRWEngine doMessageLoopWork] tick via +requestShutdownWithCompletion:, then CefShutdown + exit(0). Note: the initial fix attempt used NSApplicationDelegate.applicationShouldTerminate + .terminateLater, which builds clean but deadlocks forever (confirmed via sample: AppKit's private terminateLater event loop never services BRWMessagePump's timer, so OnBeforeClose never arrives) -- CEF's reference apps explicitly document that applicationShouldTerminate is unsupported for this reason, hence the -terminate: override instead. Two root causes, both fixed and verified. (1) The original SIGTRAP: applicationWillTerminate called CefShutdown() directly while CefBrowser instances were still alive. Fixed by overriding -[NSApplication terminate:] in BRWApplication.mm to run a close-and-wait sequence instead of AppKit's default flow -- NSApplicationDelegate.applicationShouldTerminate/.terminateLater cannot do this job (its private event-loop mode never services BRWMessagePump's timer, hanging instead of crashing; CEF's own cefclient/cefsimple reference apps document this same incompatibility). (2) A second, deeper bug the first fix exposed: OnBeforeClose was never delivered for any CefBrowser even with correct sequencing -- BRWClientHandler::RequestClose() (new single close entry point, deduped via close_requested_ so CloseBrowser() is never called twice on the same browser) must call removeFromSuperview on the CEF-created native view before CloseBrowser(), or CEF's Alloy/SetAsChild close-detection on macOS never notices the browser closed. Undocumented in CEF's own headers; matches an identical report from another Swift+CEF project (github.com/lvsti/CEF.swift#22) and a related upstream CEF report (bitbucket.org/chromiumembedded/cef/issues/2048). Verified via contained, non-interactive testing (--profiles-root + --test-no-activate test-only flags, real off-screen NSWindow/BRWBrowser instances, quit via osascript Apple Event): 5 consecutive single-window and 3 consecutive two-window quit cycles, all clean, zero new crash reports, OnBeforeClose firing for every browser. CLOSED, not viable via CEF's Safe Browsing integration -- confirmed via direct binary/header inspection of the pinned CEF 150.0.14 distribution, going further than the earlier verify-and-close sweep:

(1) Safe Browsing IS compiled in. strings on the CEF framework binary show live, real Chromium Safe Browsing code: the actual v4/v5 hash-lookup endpoints (safebrowsing.googleapis.com/v4, /v5/hashes:search), clientreport/realtime + enterprise reporting endpoints, and genuine preference names (safebrowsing.enabled, safebrowsing.enhanced) -- this is not stripped-out or stubbed code.

(2) It is gated by a Google API key at runtime (google_apis::GetAPIKey(), confirmed via the GOOGLE_API_KEY / GOOGLE_DEFAULT_CLIENT_ID / GOOGLE_DEFAULT_CLIENT_SECRET env-var strings and the IDS_MISSING_GOOGLE_API_KEYS resource string Chromium itself shows when missing). This is a real, runtime-settable env var (no rebuild needed) -- but Google restricts issuance of a working Safe Browsing key to third-party/non-Chrome-branded embedders, so Brady obtaining one is not guaranteed and is outside this codebase's control.

(3) NEW finding this session, the actual blocker: CEF's entire public embedder API (cef_request_handler.h and everbetter) has ZERO Safe-Browsing-specific hook of any kind -- no interstitial callback, no blocked-navigation handler, nothing named *SafeBrowsing*/*Malware*/*Phishing*/*Interstitial* anywhere in CEF's public headers. Contrast with OnCertificateError, a real documented hook CEF DOES provide for the analogous TLS-cert-error case. So even with a valid API key, there is no confirmed way for this (or any) CEF embedder to intercept a flagged navigation and show a warning -- Chromium's real SafeBrowsingBlockingPage interstitial lives in the //chrome UI layer, which Alloy-style CEF (this project's only supported window style) deliberately doesn't wire up. Wiring the key alone would very likely produce zero user-visible behavior change.

Given both a hard-to-clear external gate (the API key) AND a confirmed missing embedder hook even past that gate, this is a close-with-finding rather than a wire-it -- see browser-12m.6 for the proposed alternative (local malware/phishing domain list via the already-built BlockListCore machinery).

Implemented and committed (fc3c79b). Second, independent BlockList instance (threat domains) alongside the existing ad/tracker one, same trie/parser machinery, separate ThreatWarningSettings per profile. Interception: BRWClientHandler::OnBeforeResourceLoad -- a subresource hit is silently cancelled like an ad; a top-level (RT_MAIN_FRAME) hit hops to the UI thread and loads a red warning interstitial ('This site may be dangerous') instead, built via a Swift-registered callback (ThreatWarningPageRenderer, BlockListCore) reusing StartPageRenderer's data:-URL technique. 'Continue anyway (unsafe)' is a plain link to a reserved .invalid marker URL encoding the original blocked URL -- recognized at the same OnBeforeResourceLoad interception point, records a session-scoped (never persisted, forgotten on relaunch) bypass for that host, then re-issues the original navigation. 'Go back' is a plain history.back() button -- no new JS/message-channel plumbing needed for either. Privacy pane gets a 'Warn about dangerous sites (phishing/malware)' checkbox alongside the ad-blocker toggle, default on; private windows get it too (no settings UI of their own). Starter threat list deliberately contains only Google's own official Safe Browsing test domains, not a large hardcoded 'known phishing domains' list -- see StarterThreatList.swift's doc comment for why fabricating a large list of 'real' phishing domains from memory would be irresponsible (they rotate in days/weeks, unlike stable ad-tech infrastructure, and a stale/wrong entry could mislabel an innocent later owner). Real-world coverage is meant to come from wiring RemoteListSource (already stubbed) against URLhaus/OpenPhish/Phishing.Database later -- not done here. 8 new BlockListCore tests (40/40 total green), full app build green. Not verified via a live app launch this session -- see the separate note to team-lead about --profiles-root not isolating session.json/profiles.json; verified via code review + unit tests instead.
